## Environments in interactive SQL blocks

A normal SQL block without `exercise` uses the default environment `global`.

This means that one SQL block can create tables, and later SQL blocks can use the same tables again. In this first block, we create two global tables: `foo` and `bar`.

```{sql}
CREATE TABLE foo (id INTEGER, value INTEGER);
INSERT INTO foo VALUES (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 7);

CREATE TABLE bar (id INTEGER, value INTEGER);
INSERT INTO bar VALUES (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 8);
```

The next SQL block can access `foo`, because it was created in the global environment above.

```{sql}
SELECT value + 42 AS result
FROM foo;
```

## Exercise environments

SQL exercises use their own exercise environment by default. This helps to keep exercises separate from each other.

The setup block creates the start state for the exercise.

```{sql}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_1
CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER, name TEXT);
INSERT INTO products VALUES (1, 'Laptop'), (2, 'Mouse');
```

The learner code runs in the exercise environment. It can access the table from the setup block.

```{sql}
#| exercise: ex_1
SELECT * FROM products;
```

The check block is linked to the same exercise. It checks if the table has exactly two rows.

```{sql}
#| check: true
#| exercise: ex_1
SELECT COUNT(*) = 2 AS ok FROM products;
```

## Exercise isolation from global

Normal SQL blocks and exercise SQL blocks should not always share the same state.

The table `people` was created in the global environment. This exercise uses its own exercise environment, so it should not see `people`.

```{sql}
#| exercise: ex_isolated
SELECT * FROM people;
```

Expected result: this block should show an error, because `people` does not exist inside this exercise environment.

## Manually managing the environment

Sometimes exercises should build on each other. Quarto Live supports this with the `envir` option.

Exercises with the same manual `envir` value share the same environment. This can be used for follow-on exercises.

### Follow-on exercise 1

This exercise creates a table and inserts one value.

```{sql}
#| exercise: ex_shared_1
#| envir: myenv
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS numbers;
CREATE TABLE numbers (value INTEGER);
INSERT INTO numbers VALUES (7);
SELECT * FROM numbers;
```

### Follow-on exercise 2

This exercise uses the same environment `myenv`. It can access the table from the previous exercise and insert another value.

```{sql}
#| exercise: ex_shared_2
#| envir: myenv
INSERT INTO numbers VALUES (5);
SELECT * FROM numbers;
```

### Follow-on exercise 3

This exercise also uses `myenv`. It can see both inserted values and calculate their sum.

```{sql}
#| exercise: ex_shared_3
#| envir: myenv
SELECT SUM(value) AS total FROM numbers;
```

Expected result: the total should be `12`.

## Reusing global tables later

The tables `foo` and `bar` were created at the beginning of this document in the global SQL environment.

This later block can still access them, because normal SQL blocks without `exercise` share the same default environment `global`.

```{sql}
SELECT
  foo.value AS foo_value,
  bar.value AS bar_value,
  foo.value + bar.value AS sum_value
FROM foo
JOIN bar ON foo.id = bar.id;
```
